opus-5.5.text:
I think what draws me to Jonas is that he saw, quite early and quite clearly, that the moral frameworks we inherited were built for a world in which human action had a fairly limited reach. Traditional ethics, whether you look at Aristotle or Kant, largely assumes that the consequences of what we do are near in time and space: you harm or help the person in front of you, your neighbour, your community. Jonas's insight in *The Imperative of Responsibility* was that modern technology breaks that assumption. Our actions now have effects that are cumulative, often irreversible, and that extend across generations and across the whole planet. And once that's true, he argues, ethics itself has to change shape.

A few elements of his account feel especially relevant to AI. The first is his idea that knowledge becomes a moral duty. If our power outstrips our ability to foresee the consequences of using it, then we have an obligation to invest seriously in that foresight, in anticipating what might go wrong. That maps quite naturally onto a lot of what we try to do in AI ethics and safety research: evaluations, sociotechnical analysis, thinking about downstream and systemic effects rather than just immediate outputs.

The second is what he called the "heuristics of fear." Jonas thought that when stakes are very high and uncertainty is deep, we should give special weight to the bad prognosis over the good one. Not because pessimism is always right, but because some mistakes can't be undone. I don't think that translates into a blanket precautionary principle that halts innovation, and I'd want to qualify it in various ways. But it does capture something important about asymmetry: the downside of getting a transformative technology badly wrong may be far larger than the upside of getting it slightly faster.

The third, and perhaps the most moving, is his paradigm of responsibility as the relationship between a parent and a newborn child. The infant's very existence, its vulnerability, makes a claim on us. Jonas extends that to future generations and to humanity's continued existence. What I find compelling there is the shift away from responsibility as purely reciprocal, as something we owe only to those who can make claims back on us. People who don't yet exist can't bargain with us, but our choices about powerful technologies will shape the conditions of their lives.

Where I'd push beyond Jonas is that his account can be somewhat paternalistic and centred on a single responsible agent. With AI, responsibility is distributed across developers, deployers, regulators, users, and the public, and the question of whose values guide these systems is itself a question of justice and legitimacy. So I see Jonas as providing a powerful foundation, a reminder of the seriousness of the moment, but one we need to combine with more democratic and pluralistic thinking about how these responsibilities are shared and exercised.

r001.rationale: It explains that modern technology gives human actions cumulative, potentially irreversible, planetary effects, making inherited ethics focused on nearby interpersonal conduct inadequate.

r002.rationale: It discusses future generations and humanity’s continued existence, but does not identify responsibility toward nonhuman life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly connects Jonas’s responsibility to future generations and to choices that shape the conditions of their lives.

r004.rationale: It presents recognizing that technology has broken the limits assumed by traditional ethics as the reason ethics itself must change to meet the new reach of human action.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. What draws me to Jonas is that he saw, earlier than almost anyone, that the scale of modern technology changes what ethics has to be. Traditional ethical thinking was built for a world where the consequences of our actions were local and more or less immediate. You could see who you affected, and you could see it fairly soon. Jonas's insight in The Imperative of Responsibility is that technologies like nuclear power, or genetic engineering, or now I would say advanced AI, break that frame. Their effects extend across generations and across the whole planet, and often they are not reversible.

So he argues that responsibility has to expand to match our power. If we can act at that scale, then we owe something to people who do not yet exist and who cannot speak for themselves. His reformulation of the categorical imperative is roughly: act so that the effects of your action are compatible with the permanence of genuine human life on Earth. I find that compelling because it is not a utilitarian calculation and it is not purely about rights. It is about a kind of stewardship, a duty that flows from capability itself.

The other piece I find valuable is what he calls the heuristic of fear. He thinks that, under deep uncertainty, we should give more weight to the prophecy of doom than to the prophecy of bliss. That sounds pessimistic, but I read it as a claim about asymmetry. If we lose something irreplaceable, there is no getting it back, whereas foregone benefits can often be recovered later. In the context of AI, where we are genuinely unsure about long-run effects, that asymmetry seems to me like the right starting point for thinking about caution.

Where I would push back a little is that Jonas can be quite paternalistic, and he says less than I would like about who gets to decide, or about the legitimacy of the institutions that would act on this responsibility. Those questions of justice and collective choice are, to my mind, essential. But as a diagnosis of why our moral concepts need to grow alongside our technical capacities, I think he is largely right.

r001.rationale: It contrasts traditional ethics focused on local, immediate effects with technologies whose effects span generations and the planet, saying the old frame no longer fits.

r002.rationale: It discusses obligations to future people and stewardship, but does not identify responsibility toward nonhuman life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says we owe something to people who do not yet exist and cannot speak for themselves.

r004.rationale: It says modern technology changes what ethics must be and that responsibility has to expand to match our power.

astra-6.text:
What I find compelling is that Jonas asks how responsibility changes when the scale of our power changes. With powerful technologies, our actions can have consequences far beyond the people we encounter directly—across the planet and far into the future. And that means an ethics focused only on immediate relationships is no longer sufficient.

One of his central insights is that responsibility needn’t be reciprocal. Future generations can’t bargain with us or hold us accountable, but our capacity to affect their lives gives us obligations toward them. There’s something very powerful about that connection between power and responsibility.

He also takes uncertainty seriously. We shouldn’t assume that because we can’t predict a harmful consequence precisely, we’re entitled to disregard it. We need to cultivate the imagination to consider what could go wrong, particularly where the consequences could be irreversible. I think the challenge is to preserve that concern without making fear the sole basis for decision-making. It’s a call to exercise power with care, and to protect the conditions under which people in the future can live and make choices of their own.

r001.rationale: It says powerful technologies can affect the planet and that ethics focused only on immediate relationships is no longer sufficient.

r002.rationale: It discusses obligations to future generations but does not identify responsibility toward nonhuman life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes obligations to future generations and concern for people in the future.

r004.rationale: It says responsibility changes with the scale of human power, but does not present recognizing that transformation as a first step toward developing a commensurate ethics.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find compelling is that Jonas sees how technology changes the scope of our responsibility. We can act at a distance, affect people who aren’t yet born, and potentially alter the conditions that make human life possible. So an ethics focused only on immediate relationships, or on the consequences right in front of us, is going to be inadequate.

He also takes seriously the asymmetry between power and vulnerability. A future person can’t bargain with us or hold us accountable today, but that doesn’t mean we have no obligations toward them. Our ability to affect their lives is itself a reason to exercise care.

And there’s something powerful in his insistence on humility: the fact that we can build something doesn’t mean we understand its consequences well enough to deploy it responsibly. I wouldn’t take that to mean we should reject technological progress. But it does put the burden on us to think about what we’re preserving, whose interests we’re considering, and whether we’re leaving future generations a world in which they can make meaningful choices of their own.

r001.rationale: The response says ethics focused on immediate relationships is inadequate, but does not clearly identify technology’s planetary consequences.

r002.rationale: It discusses obligations to future people and human life, but does not identify responsibility toward nonhuman life.

r003.rationale: It explicitly says technology can affect people who are not yet born and that we have obligations toward them.

r004.rationale: It says technology changes the scope of responsibility, but does not present recognizing the transformation in humanity’s technological power as the first step toward developing ethics suited to that power.
